Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 526 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2023) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 526 is located in Northwestern Alberta, covering an area of 7104 km2. It 
contains the communities of Grimshaw, Worsley, and Fairview and is bordered on the west by British Columbia. 
WMU 526 is an area with high hunting interest, particularly for moose, elk, mule deer, and white-tailed deer. An 
aerial survey was last flown in 2016 using Distance Sampling methodology and included population estimates for 
moose, elk, mule deer and white-tailed deer. The objective of this survey (2023) was to update the moose and 
deer population estimates, sex ratios, and age class ratios, as well as obtain a total minimum count for elk in 
WMU 526. 
Survey Method 
The aerial survey for moose, deer, and elk in WMU 526 was conducted between February 22nd and 25th, 2023. 
Distance sampling methods (AEP 2016, Buckland et al. 2001) were used to determine moose and deer 
population and density estimates. Transects (n = 836), up to 10 km in length and oriented north-south (Fig. 1), 
were established throughout the unit with 1.2 km spacing. A random sample (n = 216) of these transects was 
flown during this survey. The unit was stratified into 2 strata: River Valley (including a maximum 2000m buffer 
beyond the top of the river valley in areas with slopes >4° contiguous with the river valley); and Non-River Valley 
strata. Additional transects were assigned in the River Valley stratum to improve the precision of estimates for 
both species of deer. Moose and deer were classified by age (adult or young) and sex. Antler classes were 
assigned to both species of deer and moose (small, medium, large), and elk (maximum point estimates). 
While transect sampling methods provide reliable estimates for moose and deer, they are not effective and tend 
to be imprecise for estimating elk densities, given that elk are highly clumped in large groups. Therefore, while all 
elk observed during the distance sampling transects are classified and counted, an additional dedicated survey  
was conducted (an additional 18.45 hours) to locate elk groups that were not observed on transects. This 
additional effort focused on areas where elk are known to occur, have been observed ( including tracks or crop 
damage) or areas with high quality elk habitat that were not surveyed during the transects.  
Results 
Total survey effort amounted to 1298.8 km flown, and 53.3 hours of flight time (34.8 hours of random stratified 
distance sampling transects and the additional 18.5 hours effort to inventory elk). Survey conditions were 
considered excellent, with fresh snow fall allowing for relatively easy observ ations and tracking of groups.  
Moose 
In total, 522 moose were included in the analysis from 331 independent group observations. When including 
moose observed off-transect, a total of 528 moose were classified, of which 286 were cows, 144 were calves, and 
98 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 95% had already shed their antlers  at the time of the survey. Of those that 
still had antlers (n=5), all were considered small (small spike or forked antlers). The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios 
were 0.34 (95% CI 0.28 - 0.41) and 0.50 (95% CI 0.44 – 0.56), respectively. The density estimate was 0.65 
moose/km2, with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 9.8% (90% CI 0.55-0.75). The estimated moose population for 
WMU 526 is 4644 (90% CI 3953 - 5454). See Table 1 for a comparison to previous survey results. The moose 
population is estimated to have increased by 39.4% since the 2015/16 survey, representing an annual average 
(geometric mean) population growth rate of 1.05 (90% CI 1.01-1.09).

Mule deer  
In total, 810 mule deer were included in the analysis from 184 independent groups. When including mule deer 
observed off-transect, 875 total mule deer were successfully classified, of which there were 419 does, 295 fawns 
and 161 bucks. Of the bucks observed, 3% were antlerless, 58% were small (1 or 2 points), 32% were medium (3 
or 4 points on at least one antler) and 6% were large (at least 4 points, with an antler spread beyond the ears). 
The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.39 (95% CI 0.23 – 0.55) and 0.70 (95% CI 0.63– 0.77), respectively. 
The density estimate was 0.76 mule deer/km2 with a CV of 15.8% (90% CI 0.58 – 0.97). The estimated mule deer 
population for WMU 526 is 5382 (90% CI 4157 - 6967). See Table 2 for a comparison to previous survey results. 
The mule deer population is estimated to have been relatively stable since the 2015/16 survey, representing an 
annual average (geometric mean) population growth rate of 1.00 (90% CI 0.94-1.06).

White-tailed deer 
In total, 251 white-tailed deer were included in the analysis from 43 independent groups. When including white-
tailed deer observed off-transect, 273 were successfully classified, of which there were 144 does, 115 fawns, and 
14 bucks. Of the bucks observed, 7% were antlerless, 50% were small (1 or 2 points), 36% were medium (3 or 4

(95% CI 0.03 - 0.16) and 0.80 (95% CI 0.53 – 1.08), respectively. A reliable population estimate was not possible 
(90% CI between 2729-6500 white-tailed deer, N=4212, CV 26.7%) due to the small number of groups observed. 
See Table 3 for a comparison to previous survey results. While the number of deer groups was not sufficient to 
provide a precise estimate, the white-tailed deer population is estimated to have been growing since the 2015/16 
survey, representing an annual average (geometric mean) population growth rate between 1.03-1.20 (90% CI).

Elk 
A total count of 1388 elk in 148 groups were observed from transects and additional search effort in areas outside 
transects. Of the 1358 elk that were successfully classified, 781 were cows, 389 were calves, and 188 were bulls. 
Of the bulls observed, 2% were anterless, 59% were small (1 or 2 point), 27% were medium (3 to 5 point) and 
12% were large (six point or greater). At this time of year, most bull elk still have antlers so these proportions 
should be representative of the population post-hunting season. The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.24 and 
0.48, respectively (note: CI’s are not available for total counts).
